rows.stem: Which of the following has the highest melting point ?

options.label: D
options.text: All have the same melting point

rows.solution:
p-DICHLOROBENZENE has the highest melting point.

All three isomers have identical molecular masses and nearly identical van der Waals forces, so melting point here is decided by SYMMETRY and how well the molecules PACK in the crystal.

The para isomer is the symmetrical one, with its two chlorines directly opposite each other. That symmetry lets the molecules fit closely and regularly into the lattice, so more energy is needed to pull them apart. The ortho and meta isomers are unsymmetrical, pack loosely, and melt lower.

Note that BOILING points do not follow the same rule — in the liquid there is no lattice to disrupt, so the boiling points of the three isomers are close together and the ortho isomer, being the most polar, boils highest. Packing governs melting, polarity governs boiling.

rows.stem: Sodium phenoxide when heated with \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) under pressure, followed by acidification, yields :
rows.solution:
The product is SALICYLIC ACID — this is KOLBE'S REACTION.

Sodium phenoxide is treated with carbon dioxide at about 400 K under a pressure of 4 to 7 atmospheres, and the product is acidified:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5ONa} + \mathrm{CO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COONa} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH}\)

The phenoxide ION is what makes the reaction possible: its negative charge is delocalised into the ring, raising the electron density enough for the ring to attack a molecule as weakly electrophilic as carbon dioxide. Phenol itself is not nucleophilic enough.

Substitution goes ORTHO, giving the hydroxyl and the carboxyl on adjacent carbons — which is what salicylic acid is, and what makes it the starting material for aspirin. Salicylaldehyde comes from a different reaction, the Reimer-Tiemann, which uses chloroform instead.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: A compound (A) with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\), forms a phenyl hydrazone and gives negative Tollens' and iodoform tests. The compound on reduction gives n-pentane. The compound (A) is :
rows.solution:
Compound (A) is PENTAN-3-ONE.

Take the four clues in turn, since each removes a possibility.

Forms a PHENYLHYDRAZONE: the compound has a CARBONYL group, so it is an aldehyde or a ketone. That rules out pentanol at once.

Negative TOLLENS' test: it is NOT an aldehyde, so pentanal goes.

Negative IODOFORM test: it has no \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group. Pentan-2-one has exactly that, so it goes too.

Reduction gives N-PENTANE: the carbon chain is straight and unbranched, which the remaining candidate satisfies.

Only \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}CO{-}CH_2CH_3}\) survives — a ketone, with its carbonyl at the middle carbon so that no methyl group sits beside it.

rows.stem: Benzene diazonium chloride on hydrolysis gives :
rows.solution:
Hydrolysis gives PHENOL.

Warming benzenediazonium chloride with water at about 283 K releases nitrogen gas, and the water supplies the hydroxyl:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{warm}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

What drives the reaction is the leaving group: \(\mathrm{N_2}\) is an exceptionally stable neutral molecule, and losing it as a gas removes it from the system entirely. Nothing else in organic chemistry leaves so readily, which is why diazonium salts substitute so freely.

That same property makes them the gateway to a whole family of products — chlorobenzene and bromobenzene by the Sandmeyer reaction, iodobenzene with potassium iodide, benzene itself with hypophosphorous acid. Each needs its own reagent; water alone gives the phenol.

rows.stem: Helical structure of proteins is stabilized by :
rows.solution:
The helical structure of proteins is stabilised by HYDROGEN BONDS.

In the \(\alpha\)-helix the chain coils so that the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) of each amino acid residue hydrogen bonds to the \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) of the residue four places along. These bonds run roughly parallel to the axis of the helix and hold the coil in shape.

Individually a hydrogen bond is weak, perhaps a twentieth the strength of a covalent bond — but there are very many of them, and together they hold the structure firmly. Their weakness is functional: it lets the protein be DENATURED, unwinding on heating or on a change of pH without any covalent bond breaking, which is what happens when an egg is boiled.

Covalent bonds hold the PRIMARY structure — the sequence itself, joined by peptide bonds — while these hydrogen bonds define the SECONDARY structure built on it.

rows.stem: A vitamin which plays a vital role in the clotting of blood is :
rows.solution:
VITAMIN K is essential for the clotting of blood.

Its deficiency causes an increased tendency to bleed, since blood that fails to clot does not stop flowing. It is found in green leafy vegetables, and it is fat soluble, so the body stores it.

The other three have quite different roles, each with its own deficiency disease. Vitamin A gives night blindness and xerophthalmia; vitamin D gives rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults; the B vitamins give beri-beri, pernicious anaemia and other conditions depending on which member is short.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The rate of reaction \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \longrightarrow \text{Products}\), is given by the equation \(\mathrm{r} = \mathrm{k[A]\,[B]}\). If B is taken in large excess, the order of reaction would be :
rows.solution:
The order becomes ONE.

The true rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\), overall order 2. But when B is present in LARGE EXCESS, so much of it is there that the small amount consumed leaves its concentration essentially UNCHANGED throughout the reaction.

A constant quantity can be folded into the rate constant:
\(\text{Rate} = (k[\mathrm{B}])[\mathrm{A}] = k'[\mathrm{A}]\) where \(k' = k[\mathrm{B}]\)

The measured order is then 1 — and such a reaction is called PSEUDO FIRST ORDER.

The classic example is the acid hydrolysis of an ester in dilute solution: water is both reactant and solvent, so vastly in excess, and the reaction is second order in principle but first order in practice. Ordering the experiment this way is a standard laboratory technique, since it isolates one reactant's order at a time.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.solution:
Isotonic solutions have the SAME OSMOTIC PRESSURE.

That is what the word means: two solutions are isotonic when, separated by a semipermeable membrane, neither drives a net flow of solvent into the other.

By the van't Hoff relation \(\pi = \mathrm{CRT}\), equal osmotic pressure at the same temperature means equal MOLAR CONCENTRATION OF PARTICLES — so two isotonic solutions need not contain the same solute, nor the same mass of it.

The medical consequence is why the term is used. A 0.9% solution of sodium chloride is isotonic with the fluid inside a red blood cell, so saline drips use exactly that strength. In a more dilute solution water would enter the cells and burst them; in a stronger one water would leave and shrivel them.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) acts as an oxidising agent in alkaline medium. When alkaline \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) is treated with KI, iodide ion is oxidised to :
rows.solution:
Iodide is oxidised to the IODATE ion, \(\mathrm{IO_3^-}\).

In ALKALINE medium permanganate is a powerful enough oxidising agent to take iodide all the way from \(-1\) to \(+5\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{I^-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} + \mathrm{IO_3^-}\)

Manganese falls from \(+7\) to \(+4\), the brown manganese dioxide precipitating out.

The MEDIUM is the whole point of the question. In ACIDIC solution the products are different — iodide is oxidised only to iodine, and manganese is reduced further, to the nearly colourless \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\). The same two reagents give different products depending on the pH, which is why an examination question always states the medium.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following transition metals does not show variable oxidation state ?
rows.solution:
SCANDIUM does not show variable oxidation states.

Scandium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^1 4s^2\), and losing all three of those electrons gives \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) with the ARGON configuration — a noble gas core with an empty \(3d\) subshell and nothing further available. So \(+3\) is its only state, and its compounds are white and diamagnetic in consequence.

Variable oxidation states arise where a metal has SEVERAL d electrons of comparable energy, so that different numbers of them can be used for bonding. Titanium reaches \(+2\), \(+3\) and \(+4\); chromium \(+2\) through \(+6\); copper \(+1\) and \(+2\).

Zinc would have served equally well as an answer, for the opposite reason: its \(3d\) subshell is completely FULL rather than nearly empty, so again only one state is available. The two ends of the series behave alike.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following complexes is a 'chelate' complex ?
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) is the chelate complex.

A CHELATE is formed when a POLYDENTATE ligand binds the same metal through more than one donor atom, closing a RING that includes the metal.

Ethylenediamine is BIDENTATE: it donates through both of its nitrogens, closing a FIVE-MEMBERED ring — two nitrogens, two carbons and the cobalt. Three such ligands close three rings.

The other three complexes use only MONODENTATE ligands — ammonia, chloride, fluoride — each binding through a single atom, so no ring is closed however many ligands are present.

Chelation confers extra stability, partly because a chelating ligand must break TWO bonds to leave rather than one, and partly because replacing several separate ligands with fewer chelating ones increases the disorder of the solution.

rows.stem: Optical isomerism is not shown by the complex :
rows.solution:
The TRANS form of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+}\) does not show optical isomerism.

Optical isomerism requires the complex to be CHIRAL — non-superimposable on its mirror image — and the usual test is whether it possesses a PLANE OF SYMMETRY.

In the trans isomer the two chlorides lie opposite each other, and a plane can be drawn containing both of them with the two ethylenediamine ligands reflected across it. The complex is superimposable on its mirror image, so it is optically inactive.

The CIS form has no such plane: its two chlorides are adjacent, and the two chelate rings are arranged as a left or a right handed propeller. It exists as a pair of enantiomers.

The other two complexes carry THREE bidentate ligands each — oxalate and ethylenediamine — and three chelate rings around an octahedral centre always give a propeller shape with no plane of symmetry, so both are optically active.

rows.stem:
Show how you will synthesise :
(a) 1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol from a suitable alkene.
(b) Cyclohexylmethanol from methanal using a suitable Grignard reagent.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — both target compounds are printed as DRAWN cyclohexane rings rather than named: (a) a ring whose top carbon bears both \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{OH}\), (b) a ring bearing \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\). I have NAMED them in the stem (1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, cyclohexylmethanol), which is a lossless reading and leaves the row fully answerable from text — the question asks for the SYNTHESIS, not the identity of the drawn compound — so this is ILLUSTRATIVE, not REQUIRED. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) 1-METHYLCYCLOHEXAN-1-OL. Acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene follows MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE, so the hydroxyl arrives at the carbon that can best support a positive charge — here the one bearing the methyl group, which gives a TERTIARY carbocation:
\(\text{1-methylcyclohexene} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{H_2O}} \text{1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol}\)

Methylenecyclohexane serves equally well, since protonating its exocyclic double bond gives the same tertiary cation.

(b) CYCLOHEXYLMETHANOL. A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon, and METHANAL is the aldehyde that gives a PRIMARY alcohol with one carbon more than the reagent:
\(\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{C_6H_{11}MgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_{11}CH_2OMgBr} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_{11}CH_2OH}\)

The reagent needed is CYCLOHEXYLMAGNESIUM BROMIDE. Working backwards is the method here: the product's carbon skeleton minus the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) carbon, which methanal supplied, is what the Grignard reagent must have carried.

rows.stem: On mixing liquid X and liquid Y, volume of the resulting solution decreases. What type of deviation from Raoult's law is shown by the resulting solution ? What change in temperature would you observe after mixing liquids X and Y ?
rows.solution:
The solution shows a NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law, and the TEMPERATURE RISES.

A contraction in volume means the molecules have moved CLOSER together on mixing, which can only happen if the interactions between UNLIKE molecules are STRONGER than those between like ones.

Stronger attractions hold the molecules in the liquid more firmly, so fewer escape and the vapour pressure is LOWER than Raoult's law predicts — a negative deviation, by definition.

The temperature follows from the same fact. Forming stronger bonds RELEASES energy, so mixing is EXOTHERMIC, \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}\mathrm{H}\) is negative, and the mixture warms. Chloroform with acetone is the standard case, the two forming a hydrogen bond between them.

The three signs move together and are worth remembering as a set: negative deviation, \(\Delta\mathrm{V}\) negative, \(\Delta\mathrm{H}\) negative. A positive deviation reverses all three, and the mixture cools.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The following data were obtained for the reaction :
\(2\mathrm{NO_2\,(g)} + \mathrm{F_2\,(g)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{NO_2F\,(g)}\)

| Experiment No. | \([\mathrm{NO_2}]/\mathrm{M}\) | \([\mathrm{F_2}]/\mathrm{M}\) | Initial rate \(\mathrm{M\ min^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(0{\cdot}2\) | \(0{\cdot}05\) | \(6 \times 10^{-3}\) |
| 2 | \(0{\cdot}4\) | \(0{\cdot}05\) | \(1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-2}\) |
| 3 | \(0{\cdot}8\) | \(0{\cdot}10\) | \(4{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-2}\) |

Determine the overall order of reaction.
rows.solution:
Write the rate law with unknown orders and find them by comparing experiments in which only one concentration changes:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{NO_2}]^p[\mathrm{F_2}]^q\)

ORDER IN \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) — compare experiments 1 and 2, where \([\mathrm{F_2}]\) is held at 0.05 M. Doubling \([\mathrm{NO_2}]\) from 0.2 to 0.4 M doubles the rate, from \(6 \times 10^{-3}\) to \(1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-2}\):
\(2^p = 2\), so \(p = 1\)

ORDER IN \(\mathrm{F_2}\) — compare experiments 2 and 3, where BOTH concentrations double and the rate rises four-fold, from \(1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-2}\) to \(4{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-2}\):
\(2^p \times 2^q = 4\)
Since \(p = 1\) accounts for a factor of 2, the remaining factor of 2 belongs to fluorine:
\(2^q = 2\), so \(q = 1\)

OVERALL ORDER \(= p + q = 1 + 1 = 2\)

Note that the order in \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) is 1 although the balanced equation shows a COEFFICIENT of 2. Order is measured, not read off the equation, and the discrepancy here is evidence that the reaction goes by more than one step.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the mechanism of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_2 = CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H}^{+}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\)
(b) Write the structures of the products obtained by heating anisole with conc. \(\mathrm{HI}\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — in sub-part (b) the substrate is printed as a DRAWN benzene ring bearing \(-\mathrm{OCH_3}\); I have NAMED it 'anisole', which is a lossless reading and does not state the answer (the question asks for the PRODUCTS of the HI cleavage), so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) MECHANISM OF ACID-CATALYSED HYDRATION, in three steps. The acid first protonates water to give the hydronium ion, \(\mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_3O^+}\), which is the proton source.

Step 1 — protonation of the alkene. The \(\pi\) electrons attack a proton, and the carbon left without them becomes a CARBOCATION. This is the SLOW, rate determining step:
\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H_3O^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 2 — nucleophilic attack by water. An oxygen lone pair attacks the positive carbon, giving a protonated alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

Step 3 — loss of a proton to a second water molecule, which regenerates the catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_3O^+}\)

The acid is a true CATALYST — consumed in step 1 and returned in step 3 — which is why only a trace is needed.

(b) Heating anisole with concentrated hydroiodic acid gives PHENOL and IODOMETHANE:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)

The oxygen is protonated first, and the iodide then attacks the METHYL carbon rather than the ring carbon. Two reasons force that choice: the bond from oxygen to the \(sp^2\) ring carbon has partial double bond character from resonance and is the stronger of the two, and a benzene ring carbon is not open to backside attack in any case.

So the cleavage is never the other way round — iodobenzene and methanol are not formed.
